3	## KeyPoints
4	
5	Question Does prenatal and infancy homevisitation by nurses reduce obesity and hypertension among mothers with very low income and their first-born offspring at 12 and 18 years following birth?
6	
7	Findings In this randomized clinical trial of 742 participants, nurse-visited female offspring had lower rates of obesity and severe obesity at age 12 and 18 years combined than their control group counterparts; nurse-visited mothers of females had lower rates of stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension at child age 12 and 18 years combined compared with their control group counterparts. No intervention effect was found for these outcomes among male offspring or mothers of males.
8	
9	Meaning These findings suggest that prenatal and infancy home visitation holds promise for reducing obesity among female offspring living in extreme poverty and reducing their mothers' hypertension.

35	## Introduction
36	
37	Poverty and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) pose substantial risks for a range of health problems, 1-4 including obesity among female children and adolescents 5 and hypertensive disorders among adults. 6-10 These disparities are especially pronounced among females and Black individuals. 11-13 Obesity and hypertension are major public health concerns because they increase the risk for a variety of chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and kidney failure, as well as premature mortality. 11,14,15 Addressing these conditions among people living with very low income, and especially among Black individuals, is a public health imperative. 16
38	
39	The Nurse-Family Partnership (NFP) is a program of prenatal and infant and toddler home visiting by nurses designed to improve outcomes of (1) pregnancy, (2) child health and development, and (3) maternal health and life course (eMethods in Supplement 2). 17,18 The NFP has been tested in a series of randomized clinical trials in the US for different populations living in different contexts, with replicated benefits found in these domains in at least 2 of these trials. 17,18 Many program effects were most pronounced among families experiencing the greatest adversity. 18 The focus of the current investigation is on participants in Memphis, Tennessee, living in deep poverty and in resource-poor neighborhoods. 19 Program effects on maternal and child health in this trial have been reported for prenatal health (including pregnancy-induced hypertension), 19 child health and development, 19-23 and maternal health and life course. 19-21,24-26
40

input.text:
Of the 742 participants randomized (mean [SD] age, 18.1 [3.2] years), we completed interviews with 594 mothers (NFP, 187 participants; control, 407 participants) and 578 offspring (NFP, 180 participants; control, 398 participants) at child age 12 years and 618 mothers (NFP, 192 participants; control, 426 participants) and 629 offspring (NFP, 194 participants; control, 435 participants) at child age 18 years.

in the control group, a mean (SD) proportion of 0.18 (0.39) at age 12 and 18 years had severe obesity, and the intervention reduced the risk of obesity by more than half at age 12 years (adjusted relative risk [ARR], 0.396; 95% CI, 0.169-0.931; P =.007) and more than 40% at age 18 years (ARR, 0.561; 95% CI, 0.293-1.075; P =.05).

a mean (SD) proportion of 0.25 (0.43) had obesity and 0.12 (0.33) had severe obesity at both ages, with NFP reducing the female offspring risk of obesity by 55% compared with the control group (ARR, 0.449; 95% CI, 0.234-0.858; P = .003) and the risk of severe obesity by 81% (ARR, 0.185; 95%CI, 0.046-0.748; P < .001).

the mean (SD) proportion of females and males with obesity at age 12 years was 0.32 (0.47) and 0.21 (0.41), respectively.

of mothers of female offspring in the control group, a mean (SD) proportion of 0.57 (0.50) had stage 1 hypertension and 0.27 (0.44) had stage 2 hypertension, with NFP reducing the risk for stage 1 hypertension by 39% (ARR, 0.613; 95% CI, 0.440-0.855; P = .001) and the risk for stage 2 hypertension by 79% (ARR, 0.217; 95% CI, 0.081-0.582; P < .001).

Nurse-visited male offspring had longer mean gestations than control group male offspring (least squares mean difference [LSMD], 0.76 weeks; 95% CI, 0.150-1.359 weeks; P = .02), as well as higher birth weights (LSMD, 191.37 g; 95% CI, 55.01-327.75 g; P = .006). Moreover, the prevalence of preterm birth was higher among controls than the NFP group (ARR, 0.663; 95% CI, 0.455-0.965; P = .02).

Nurse-visited mothers had a lower mean arterial blood pressure at birth than control group mothers (LSMD, -2.226 mm Hg; 95% CI, -4.091 to -0.362; P = .02) and lower prevalence of any health condition at child age 18 years (12% reduction; ARR, 0.879; 95% CI, 0.775-0.997; P = .04). These differences were concentrated in mothers of females (mean arterial blood pressure: LSMD, -4.064 mm Hg [95% CI, -6.727 to -1.401; P = .003]; any health condition: ARR, 0.721 [95% CI, 0.588-0.884; P = .001]). nurse-visited mothers of females reported fewer counts of health conditions at offspring age 18 years than their control group counterparts (LSMD, -0.553; 95% CI, -0.966 to -0.140; P = .009).

A simple mediation analysis suggested that 27.3% of the NFP effect for stage 1 hypertension in mothers of females at child age 18 years was mediated by a reduction in stage 1 hypertension at child age 12 years; this increased to 30.3% when we also included maternal obesity at child age 12 years. Additionally, 75.4% of the NFP effect on female offspring obesity at age 18 years was mediated by a reduction in obesity at age 12 years; this increased to 82.6% when we also included overweight at 2 years of age.

in the control group, having a mother with severe hypertension was associated with a higher chance (11.3 correlation coefficient) of having a female child with severe hypertension. This association was absent in the treated group, with a significant 0.188 treatment difference in the intergenerational correlation coefficients.

Of the mothers interviewed at child age 12 years, 3 (0.5%) self-reported their race as Aleut, Eskimo, or American Indian; 0 as Asian or Pacific Islander; 559 (94.1%) as Black; and 32 (5.4%) as White. All 618 reported non-Hispanic ethnicity. Of the mothers interviewed at child age 18 years, 5 (0.8%) self-reported their race as Aleut, Eskimo, or American Indian; 0 as Asian or Pacific Islander; 578 (93.5%) as Black; and 35 (5.7%) as White. One mother (0.2%) reported Hispanic ethnicity, and 617 mothers (98.8%) reported non-Hispanic ethnicity.

unchecked.reason: verify_power_analysis requires the effect size, alpha, target power and n actually used; the paper states only 'at least 80% power (alpha = .05) for the majority of outcomes' without naming the effect size assumed or which outcomes qualify. Inputs are in the unavailable supplement, so the calculation cannot be reproduced. Separately worth flagging editorially: these are EX-POST (post hoc) power calculations, computed from observed effects, which are widely regarded as uninformative about a completed study.

Supplement 2 not provided. This withholds the inverse-probability-weighting robustness analysis (eTable 9), the unbalanced-covariate robustness check (eTable 10), the self-report-exclusion robustness checks (eTables 11-12), the mediation analysis (eTable 7) and the intergenerational correlation analysis (eTable 8) -- the last being the source of the impossible 11.3 correlation coefficient, which therefore cannot be diagnosed further.

unchecked.location: Figure (quantile regression treatment effects, panels A-F)
unchecked.reason: Vector-drawn quantile-regression plots with 90% CI bands and no numeric values in the caption or body. No coefficients, standard errors or deciles are reported anywhere in text, so nothing was digitizable to a checkable statistic. Any values read off the marks would be tier-2 figure_pixels provenance and barred from the exact-arithmetic tools in any case.

Reported as bare point estimates with no standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values or component coefficients. Gelbach decomposition inputs are in eTable 7 (unavailable). No validated tool can test a proportion-mediated figure without its variance components.

unchecked.location: Per-arm sample sizes for every cell of Tables 1-4
unchecked.reason: Never reported -- only a combined row N. This is what defeated DEBIT (see finding debit_binary_proportions_indeterminate) and it also blocks recalc_independent_t, recalc_chi_squared and reconstruct_2x2 on the group proportions, since no cell counts can be recovered. The single most consequential reporting omission for verifiability in this paper.

unchecked.location: Maternal age at randomization, mean (SD) 18.1 (3.2), n=742
unchecked.reason: GRIM and GRIMMER were deliberately NOT run. Age in years is a continuous measure and the paper does not state it was recorded as whole years; applying integer-scale tools to a continuous variable is the most common route to a false accusation. Even had it been integer-valued, GRIM granularity at n=742 (1/742 = 0.0013) is far finer than the reported 1 decimal place, so the test would be vacuous.

unchecked.location: Romano-Wolf multiple-hypothesis-testing p-values (69 MHT values across Tables 1-4)
unchecked.reason: No validated tool reproduces a bootstrap stepdown correction. The MHT column was compared against the uncorrected p column by direct inspection only (see finding mht_p_smaller_than_uncorrected_p); the corrected values themselves could not be recalculated without the 1000-replication bootstrap and the underlying data.

unchecked.location: Multiplicity across the full analysis (69 ARR tests in main tables plus supplementary outcomes)
unchecked.reason: Recorded as an anatomy fact rather than a tool finding: the Romano-Wolf correction was applied WITHIN 6 blocks of 3 outcomes per table, i.e. within-table only, not across the 4 tables or across the sex strata jointly. No tool in the suite evaluates whether a stated correction's blocking structure is adequate for the full family of tests, so this is flagged for editorial judgment. Relevant context: the paper states these outcomes were not primary or secondary in the original protocol and that sex was not hypothesized as a moderator.

hypotheses.statement: Prenatal and infancy nurse home visitation reduces offspring obesity and severe obesity at ages 12 and 18 years, with the effect concentrated in female offspring.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: This study examines the Memphis program's effects on maternal and offspring obesity and hypertension at offspring ages 12 and 18 years, aspects of health that were not primary or secondary outcomes in the original study design or the follow-ups at child ages 12 and 18 years.

hypotheses.statement: Prenatal and infancy nurse home visitation reduces maternal stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension at child ages 12 and 18 years, with the effect concentrated in mothers of female offspring.

hypotheses.statement: Offspring sex moderates the intervention effect on obesity and hypertension.

hypotheses.statement: Health improvements at child age 12 years mediate sustained treatment effects at child age 18 years, and NFP breaks intergenerational persistence in hypertension.
